Fixed via a new pilotHasFinancialArtifacts() helper checking all three tables by their shared metadata->>pilotApplicationId marker. (3) NO CONCURRENCY GUARD — bindPilotOrganization/rebindPilotOrganization performed read-then-update with no row lock, so two concurrent verifications for different orgs (or a rebind racing a concurrent commercial-transition creating a financial artifact) could both observe stale state; last writer wins. Fixed: both functions now take SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on the pilot row inside withSystemContext's real transaction, and commercial-transition's monetization transaction takes the same lock before creating any artifact, so all three now serialize against each other. (4) BROKEN GENERIC DELETE — the shared factory's DELETE soft-deletes by writing status='archived' whenever a status column exists, but round 21 made pilot status exclusively FSM-governed by commercial-transition, and pilot_status has no 'archived' value at all — the exported DELETE handler both violated the new FSM rule and would fail against the enum if ever invoked. Fixed by removing the DELETE export entirely (405 by default); a real archive/close action belongs in the commercial-transition FSM, not a generic soft-delete. Also corrected overstated language from round 21: rebindPilotOrganization's logging is a structured logger.warn call, not yet a durable audit_logs row — doc comments now say "logged for traceability," not "audited." Round 23 closed three further gaps a deeper live-source review found directly inside this trust boundary: (1) LOCKED TOO LATE — commercial-transition previously loaded the application, derived verifiedOrganizationId/responses/fromState, and validated the FSM transition BEFORE entering the transaction that locks the row, then used those pre-lock values inside the lock — so a rebind that committed between the initial read and the lock being acquired left the transition using a stale verified-org/commercial-state snapshot. Fixed: the row is now re-SELECTed with FOR UPDATE as the FIRST statement inside the transaction, and verifiedOrganizationId, responses, fromState, and the proposal are ALL derived from that locked read; a new CommercialTransitionRejected error class lets expected rejections (404/409/400) discovered after locking roll back the transaction and still return the exact intended HTTP response. The earlier pre-lock read is now only a cheap existence + role-tier check, never a source of financial or FSM decisions. (2) RESPONSES REMAINED A MIXED-TRUST STORE — round 22 protected only responses.organizationId from steward PATCH, leaving responses.commercialState (drives FSM validation), responses.subscriptionPlanId (selects the billing plan on activation), commercialTransitionHistory, pilotIntelligence, qualification/opportunity scores, artifact-version metadata, and commercialMonetization all editable — contradicting round 21's claim that commercial state is FSM-controlled. Fixed: preserveClaimedOrganizationOnPatch was generalized into preserveServerOwnedResponsesFields, which restores ALL server-owned responses keys (organizationId plus the full commercial/scoring/artifact list above) to their existing values on every PATCH, while leaving every other responses key ordinarily editable. (3) TENANT AUTHORIZATION STILL FOLLOWED THE CLAIM AFTER VERIFICATION/REBIND — the ownership pre-check loaded only responses and authorized via getPilotClaimedOrganizationId, never verifiedOrganizationId, so after a platform rebind moved the authoritative owner from Org A to Org B, Org A stewards still passed the tenant ownership check and Org B stewards did not — the rebind changed financial identity but not tenant authorization. Fixed: a new getPilotEffectiveOrganizationId () (verifiedOrganizationId ?? claimedOrganizationId) is now the ONLY value application-layer ownership checks use (enforcePilotOwnership/withPilotOwnership, and loadPilotApplicationForOwnershipCheck now also selects verifiedOrganizationId to make this possible); once a verified owner exists it is authoritative everywhere, including after a rebind. The eventual tenant RLS policy for this table must encode the SAME effective-owner rule (COALESCE(verified_organization_id, (responses->>'organizationId')::uuid) = current_setting(...)), not the claim-only JSONB expression sketched in earlier rounds. Round 24 was structural rather than another field-by-field patch: (1) PUBLIC-CREATE PROVENANCE BYPASS — the public intake POST's responses: z.record(z.unknown()) schema let an unauthenticated applicant seed a brand-new row with the SAME reserved keys rounds 22-23 protected on UPDATE (commercialState, subscriptionPlanId, qualification scores, artifact metadata, ...), and the PATCH-time protection then faithfully preserved that attacker-seeded value forever — protecting an update is meaningless if creation was never sanitized. Fixed by extracting a SINGLE canonical registry (lib/pilot/responses-authority.ts's RESERVED_RESPONSES_KEYS) used by BOTH the public POST (sanitizeResponsesForPublicCreate strips every reserved key except organizationId, the intentionally untrusted claim) and the PATCH path, so there is exactly one place to update when a new governed route starts writing a new responses key. (2) INCOMPLETE REGISTRY — round 23's list missed reference-profile/route.ts's 4 reference-version keys (pilotReferenceVersions, latestPilotReferenceVersionId, latestPilotReferenceChecksum, latestPilotReferenceUpdatedAt) entirely — verified via a full-repo inventory of every '.update(pilotApplications)' call site this round; all 4 now reserved. championScore/activityScore deliberately remain unreserved — verified no route ever WRITES them (only reads, as optional bounded-impact scoring inputs with a computed fallback when absent), so reserving them would remove the only way they can ever be set; documented as a deliberate decision, not an oversight. (3) PATCH COULD STILL REVERT FRESHLY COMMITTED SERVER STATE — the round 22/23 beforeUpdate hook read the current row, copied reserved values into the merged object, then replaced the WHOLE responses column — a lost-update race if commercial-transition committed a reserved-key change between that read and this PATCH's write (the PATCH would silently revert it). Fixed by replacing the read-copy-write model with an atomic JSONB MERGE: crudRoutes() gained a mergeJsonColumns option (lib/api/crud-factory.ts) that locks the row FOR UPDATE, strips reserved keys from the client's responses fragment (never reading or reproducing their current values), and issues 'responses || fragment' rather than a full-column replace — a concurrent write to any key absent from the fragment can never be reverted, because the PATCH's SQL never mentions that key at all. Round 25 closed 4 structural gaps the reviewer found in this model: (1) the merge helper silently fell back to a full-column REPLACE for a non-object responses value (e.g. an array or null) — buildMergeSetValues() now throws via validateMergeJsonColumnValues() for any mergeJsonColumns value that is not a plain object, closing a direct reserved-state destruction primitive; (2) intelligence/artifacts/reference-profile's POST handlers ran an UNLOCKED read-modify-write on the whole responses column — a server-writer-vs-server-writer race against commercial-transition's own locked write — now rewritten onto a new withLockedPilotMutation() primitive (lib/pilot/pilot-mutation.ts) that locks the row FOR UPDATE, re-authorizes the effective owner under that SAME lock, and merges only the specific keys each route owns (pilotIntelligence; the 4 artifact-version fields; the 4 reference-version fields), never the whole column; (3) the generic CRUD PATCH's ownership pre-check ran on an unlocked read BEFORE crud-factory's own row lock — a concurrent platform rebind could move ownership in that gap — closed via a new lockedAuthCheck CrudOptions hook that re-evaluates authorizePilotAccess against the row the SAME transaction just locked; (4) commercial-transition derived real contract/invoice amounts from applicant-supplied member_count (steward-PATCH-editable) and selected a subscription plan via an ambiguous "any active plan" fallback since responses.subscriptionPlanId had no governed writer — both replaced by a platform-approved commercial-terms snapshot (verified_member_count, verified_pilot_amount, verified_subscription_plan_id, commercial_terms_approved_by/at columns; lib/pilot/commercial-terms-authority.ts's approveCommercialTerms, the ONLY writer, gated behind system_admin+ like verify-organization/rebind-organization) that every financial-artifact-creating transition (contract_sent, invoice_issued, subscription_active) now requires before proceeding. Round 26 closed lifecycle/governance defects an independent review found in round 25's own delivery: (1) ORM AUTHORITY DOCTRINE VIOLATION — round 25 added the 5 commercial-terms columns via a standalone raw SQL file in apps/union-eyes/db/migrations/, which is BOTH a frozen, read-only historical Drizzle lineage (db/migrations/.lineage-frozen — new files there are explicitly prohibited per db/migrations/LINEAGE-FROZEN.md) AND a violation of this table's own Django-canonical authority (this table is a Django-canonical business entity per docs/categories/platform-and-operations/architecture/orm-governance/master-orm-governance-index.md; Drizzle's marketing.ts is a TYPE MIRROR only). Fixed: deleted the standalone SQL file; added the 5 fields to Django's PilotApplications model (backend/content/models.py) and a real Django migration (backend/content/migrations/0003_pilotapplications_commercial_terms.py), validated via `manage.py makemigrations --check --dry-run` + `manage.py check` (both clean for this table; a small set of PRE-EXISTING, unrelated drift in other Django apps — auth_core, content/documents-rename, core, services, unions — remains exactly as it was before this round, confirmed unchanged, not silently fixed as part of this round). (2) STALE DEMO SCHEMA PREFLIGHT — backend/content/management/commands/check_pilot_schema.py still only checked the 3 round-21 verified-organization columns, so it could report success on a database where every round-25 commercial-transition call to a financial-artifact-creating state would 500 on "column does not exist"; expanded to check all 8 columns across both migrations, with a column-to-migration map so a failure names the exact migration(s) still needed. (3) COMMERCIAL TERMS APPROVED BUT NOT LIFECYCLE-BOUND — approveCommercialTerms() previously allowed re-approval with DIFFERENT values indefinitely, even after a contract/invoice/subscription had already been created from a prior approval — an authoritative-state/ledger-state divergence with no record of which approval produced which artifact. Fixed: exported the existing pilotHasFinancialArtifacts() census (lib/pilot/pilot-ownership.ts, previously private) and made approveCommercialTerms() refuse ANY further approval (409, even with identical values) once a real financial artifact exists for the pilot, checked AFTER the SAME row lock used for the write (TOCTOU-safe against a concurrent commercial-transition). (4) TERMS SURVIVED ORGANIZATION REBIND — rebindPilotOrganization() changed verifiedOrganizationId/verifiedBy/verifiedAt but left a prior organization's approved commercial terms intact, so commercial-transition could create the NEW organization's financial artifacts from an approval made under the PREVIOUS organization's context. Fixed: rebind now unconditionally clears verifiedMemberCount/verifiedPilotAmount/verifiedSubscriptionPlanId/commercialTermsApprovedBy/commercialTermsApprovedAt whenever the verified organization actually changes (never for the idempotent same-org no-op path), forcing fresh approval under the new organization's context before any further financial-artifact-creating transition. Also closed two smaller financial-hardening gaps: pilotAmount is now validated on its NORMALIZED (toFixed(2)-rounded) value — at least $0.01 and within numeric(12,2) bounds — not the raw pre-rounding input (a raw value like 0.001 was previously positive but normalized to "0.00"); and commercial-transition's subscription_active branch now revalidates the approved plan's isActive status inside the SAME locked transaction at ACTIVATION time, not just at approval time, staging the activation only (never silently proceeding) if the plan has since been deactivated. Round 27 closed 3 further lifecycle gaps an independent review found in round 26's own delivery: (1) TERMS APPROVABLE BEFORE ORGANIZATION VERIFICATION — round 26 correctly cleared commercial terms on rebindPilotOrganization (an already-verified org changing to a different one), but approveCommercialTerms() never checked verifiedOrganizationId at all, so terms could be approved while the pilot's organization was still NULL (never yet verified), then bindPilotOrganization() (the first-time NULL -> org bind, a SEPARATE function from rebind) could bind it afterward with the pre-existing approval never evaluated in that organization's context. Fixed: approveCommercialTerms() now loads verifiedOrganizationId inside its own locked pilot read and returns 409 if absent, closing the gap for the FIRST bind the same way round 26 closed it for rebinds. (2) ACKNOWLEDGED POST-ARTIFACT REBIND CREATED A PERMANENT DEAD END — rebindPilotOrganization() still permitted an organization change after financial artifacts existed via an acknowledgeFinancialArtifacts=true escape hatch, which then unconditionally cleared the pilot's commercial terms (round 26) — but round 26 ALSO made approveCommercialTerms() refuse EVERY further approval once any financial artifact exists. Combined, an acknowledged rebind cleared the terms and then made re-approving them permanently impossible, since the pre-existing artifact is never deleted. Fixed: removed the acknowledgeFinancialArtifacts escape hatch entirely — rebindPilotOrganization() now unconditionally refuses (409, no override) once any real financial artifact exists; a post-artifact organization correction requires a dedicated financial-correction workflow that does not exist yet, not this function with an acknowledgement flag. (3) FINANCIAL ARTIFACTS DID NOT CARRY THE APPROVAL THAT PRODUCED THEM — commercialContracts/platformInvoices/orgSubscriptions metadata recorded only { source, pilotApplicationId }, so once an organization correction cleared the pilot row's own terms (round 26), a previously-created contract or invoice could no longer prove which approved commercial snapshot produced it. Fixed: new buildCommercialTermsSnapshot() (lib/pilot/commercialization-wave1.ts, reusing the SAME deterministic DJB2-style checksum already used for artifact/reference version records) builds an immutable { verifiedOrganizationId, verifiedMemberCount, verifiedPilotAmount, verifiedSubscriptionPlanId, commercialTermsApprovedBy, commercialTermsApprovedAt } snapshot plus a commercialTermsFingerprint hash, stamped into the metadata of every commercialContracts / platformInvoices / platformInvoiceLineItems / orgSubscriptions row CREATED (not merely updated) by commercial-transition — the pilot row's own terms remain the CURRENT authoritative snapshot; each artifact's stamped snapshot is the HISTORICAL one in effect at the moment that specific artifact was created, and the two are expected to diverge over time after any correction, which is exactly what this makes provable. Round 28 closed the one concrete provenance bypass an independent review found in round 27's own creation-side stamping: SUBSCRIPTION PROVENANCE WAS MUTABLE BY AN ORDINARY STEWARD — app/api/billing/subscriptions/[id]/route.ts's PATCH accepted `metadata: z.record(z.unknown()).optional()` at steward-level auth and wrote `.set({ ...body, updatedAt: new Date() })`, a full-column replace of orgSubscriptions.metadata — so a same-org steward could erase (`{"metadata":{}}`) or forge (fabricated snapshot + fingerprint) the commercialTermsSnapshot/commercialTermsFingerprint round 27 stamps at creation, defeating the provenance claim entirely (the fingerprint is deliberately non-cryptographic and lives in the SAME mutable JSON object it is meant to attest, so forging both together is trivial once the column itself is writable). Reviewed and confirmed contracts/invoices have no equivalent exposed arbitrary-metadata PATCH in this codebase — the defect was subscription-only. Fixed: the route now strips both server-owned keys from the client's metadata fragment (never trusting a client-supplied value for either, whether erased or forged) and restores each one from the row's CURRENT value (never an earlier read, never fabricated if the row never had it) — an ordinary steward may still freely edit any OTHER metadata key, but never these two. Also hardened the financial-transition gate itself: it previously verified verifiedMemberCount/verifiedPilotAmount/verifiedSubscriptionPlanId (round 25-27) but only TYPE-CAST commercialTermsApprovedBy/commercialTermsApprovedAt as non-null when building the provenance snapshot rather than actually checking them at runtime — since both DB columns are nullable, a partially populated or drifted row could in principle produce an artifact with incomplete provenance; the 409 gate now requires both fields non-null before any financial-artifact-creating transition, same as the other three fields.

Fixed via a new crud-factory beforeUpdate hook (mirrors the existing beforeCreate pattern) wired to a new exported, directly-unit-tested preserveClaimedOrganizationOnPatch(), which forces the claimed organizationId back to the row's existing value on every PATCH regardless of what the client sends, while leaving every other responses subfield ordinarily editable. Fixed via a new pilotHasFinancialArtifacts() helper checking all three tables by their shared metadata->>pilotApplicationId marker. (3) NO CONCURRENCY GUARD — bindPilotOrganization/rebindPilotOrganization performed read-then-update with no row lock, so two concurrent verifications for different orgs (or a rebind racing a concurrent commercial-transition creating a financial artifact) could both observe stale state; last writer wins. Fixed: both functions now take SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on the pilot row inside withSystemContext's real transaction, and commercial-transition's monetization transaction takes the same lock before creating any artifact, so all three now serialize against each other. (4) BROKEN GENERIC DELETE — the shared factory's DELETE soft-deletes by writing status='archived' whenever a status column exists, but round 21 made pilot status exclusively FSM-governed by commercial-transition, and pilot_status has no 'archived' value at all — the exported DELETE handler both violated the new FSM rule and would fail against the enum if ever invoked. Fixed by removing the DELETE export entirely (405 by default); a real archive/close action belongs in the commercial-transition FSM, not a generic soft-delete. Also corrected overstated language from round 21: rebindPilotOrganization's logging is a structured logger.warn call, not yet a durable audit_logs row — doc comments now say "logged for traceability," not "audited." Round 23 closed three further gaps a deeper live-source review found directly inside this trust boundary: (1) LOCKED TOO LATE — commercial-transition previously loaded the application, derived verifiedOrganizationId/responses/fromState, and validated the FSM transition BEFORE entering the transaction that locks the row, then used those pre-lock values inside the lock — so a rebind that committed between the initial read and the lock being acquired left the transition using a stale verified-org/commercial-state snapshot. Fixed: the row is now re-SELECTed with FOR UPDATE as the FIRST statement inside the transaction, and verifiedOrganizationId, responses, fromState, and the proposal are ALL derived from that locked read; a new CommercialTransitionRejected error class lets expected rejections (404/409/400) discovered after locking roll back the transaction and still return the exact intended HTTP response. The earlier pre-lock read is now only a cheap existence + role-tier check, never a source of financial or FSM decisions. (2) RESPONSES REMAINED A MIXED-TRUST STORE — round 22 protected only responses.organizationId from steward PATCH, leaving responses.commercialState (drives FSM validation), responses.subscriptionPlanId (selects the billing plan on activation), commercialTransitionHistory, pilotIntelligence, qualification/opportunity scores, artifact-version metadata, and commercialMonetization all editable — contradicting round 21's claim that commercial state is FSM-controlled. Fixed: preserveClaimedOrganizationOnPatch was generalized into preserveServerOwnedResponsesFields, which restores ALL server-owned responses keys (organizationId plus the full commercial/scoring/artifact list above) to their existing values on every PATCH, while leaving every other responses key ordinarily editable. (3) TENANT AUTHORIZATION STILL FOLLOWED THE CLAIM AFTER VERIFICATION/REBIND — the ownership pre-check loaded only responses and authorized via getPilotClaimedOrganizationId, never verifiedOrganizationId, so after a platform rebind moved the authoritative owner from Org A to Org B, Org A stewards still passed the tenant ownership check and Org B stewards did not — the rebind changed financial identity but not tenant authorization. Fixed: a new getPilotEffectiveOrganizationId () (verifiedOrganizationId ?? claimedOrganizationId) is now the ONLY value application-layer ownership checks use (enforcePilotOwnership/withPilotOwnership, and loadPilotApplicationForOwnershipCheck now also selects verifiedOrganizationId to make this possible); once a verified owner exists it is authoritative everywhere, including after a rebind. The eventual tenant RLS policy for this table must encode the SAME effective-owner rule (COALESCE(verified_organization_id, (responses->>'organizationId')::uuid) = current_setting(...)), not the claim-only JSONB expression sketched in earlier rounds. Round 24 was structural rather than another field-by-field patch: (1) PUBLIC-CREATE PROVENANCE BYPASS — the public intake POST's responses: z.record(z.unknown()) schema let an unauthenticated applicant seed a brand-new row with the SAME reserved keys rounds 22-23 protected on UPDATE (commercialState, subscriptionPlanId, qualification scores, artifact metadata, ...), and the PATCH-time protection then faithfully preserved that attacker-seeded value forever — protecting an update is meaningless if creation was never sanitized. Fixed by extracting a SINGLE canonical registry (lib/pilot/responses-authority.ts's RESERVED_RESPONSES_KEYS) used by BOTH the public POST (sanitizeResponsesForPublicCreate strips every reserved key except organizationId, the intentionally untrusted claim) and the PATCH path, so there is exactly one place to update when a new governed route starts writing a new responses key. (2) INCOMPLETE REGISTRY — round 23's list missed reference-profile/route.ts's 4 reference-version keys (pilotReferenceVersions, latestPilotReferenceVersionId, latestPilotReferenceChecksum, latestPilotReferenceUpdatedAt) entirely — verified via a full-repo inventory of every '.update(pilotApplications)' call site this round; all 4 now reserved. championScore/activityScore deliberately remain unreserved — verified no route ever WRITES them (only reads, as optional bounded-impact scoring inputs with a computed fallback when absent), so reserving them would remove the only way they can ever be set; documented as a deliberate decision, not an oversight. (3) PATCH COULD STILL REVERT FRESHLY COMMITTED SERVER STATE — the round 22/23 beforeUpdate hook read the current row, copied reserved values into the merged object, then replaced the WHOLE responses column — a lost-update race if commercial-transition committed a reserved-key change between that read and this PATCH's write (the PATCH would silently revert it). Fixed by replacing the read-copy-write model with an atomic JSONB MERGE: crudRoutes() gained a mergeJsonColumns option (lib/api/crud-factory.ts) that locks the row FOR UPDATE, strips reserved keys from the client's responses fragment (never reading or reproducing their current values), and issues 'responses || fragment' rather than a full-column replace — a concurrent write to any key absent from the fragment can never be reverted, because the PATCH's SQL never mentions that key at all. Round 25 closed 4 structural gaps the reviewer found in this model: (1) the merge helper silently fell back to a full-column REPLACE for a non-object responses value (e.g. an array or null) — buildMergeSetValues() now throws via validateMergeJsonColumnValues() for any mergeJsonColumns value that is not a plain object, closing a direct reserved-state destruction primitive; (2) intelligence/artifacts/reference-profile's POST handlers ran an UNLOCKED read-modify-write on the whole responses column — a server-writer-vs-server-writer race against commercial-transition's own locked write — now rewritten onto a new withLockedPilotMutation() primitive (lib/pilot/pilot-mutation.ts) that locks the row FOR UPDATE, re-authorizes the effective owner under that SAME lock, and merges only the specific keys each route owns (pilotIntelligence; the 4 artifact-version fields; the 4 reference-version fields), never the whole column; (3) the generic CRUD PATCH's ownership pre-check ran on an unlocked read BEFORE crud-factory's own row lock — a concurrent platform rebind could move ownership in that gap — closed via a new lockedAuthCheck CrudOptions hook that re-evaluates authorizePilotAccess against the row the SAME transaction just locked; (4) commercial-transition derived real contract/invoice amounts from applicant-supplied member_count (steward-PATCH-editable) and selected a subscription plan via an ambiguous "any active plan" fallback since responses.subscriptionPlanId had no governed writer — both replaced by a platform-approved commercial-terms snapshot (verified_member_count, verified_pilot_amount, verified_subscription_plan_id, commercial_terms_approved_by/at columns; lib/pilot/commercial-terms-authority.ts's approveCommercialTerms, the ONLY writer, gated behind system_admin+ like verify-organization/rebind-organization) that every financial-artifact-creating transition (contract_sent, invoice_issued, subscription_active) now requires before proceeding. Round 26 closed lifecycle/governance defects an independent review found in round 25's own delivery: (1) ORM AUTHORITY DOCTRINE VIOLATION — round 25 added the 5 commercial-terms columns via a standalone raw SQL file in apps/union-eyes/db/migrations/, which is BOTH a frozen, read-only historical Drizzle lineage (db/migrations/.lineage-frozen — new files there are explicitly prohibited per db/migrations/LINEAGE-FROZEN.md) AND a violation of this table's own Django-canonical authority (this table is a Django-canonical business entity per docs/categories/platform-and-operations/architecture/orm-governance/master-orm-governance-index.md; Drizzle's marketing.ts is a TYPE MIRROR only). Fixed: deleted the standalone SQL file; added the 5 fields to Django's PilotApplications model (backend/content/models.py) and a real Django migration (backend/content/migrations/0003_pilotapplications_commercial_terms.py), validated via `manage.py makemigrations --check --dry-run` + `manage.py check` (both clean for this table; a small set of PRE-EXISTING, unrelated drift in other Django apps — auth_core, content/documents-rename, core, services, unions — remains exactly as it was before this round, confirmed unchanged, not silently fixed as part of this round). (2) STALE DEMO SCHEMA PREFLIGHT — backend/content/management/commands/check_pilot_schema.py still only checked the 3 round-21 verified-organization columns, so it could report success on a database where every round-25 commercial-transition call to a financial-artifact-creating state would 500 on "column does not exist"; expanded to check all 8 columns across both migrations, with a column-to-migration map so a failure names the exact migration(s) still needed. (3) COMMERCIAL TERMS APPROVED BUT NOT LIFECYCLE-BOUND — approveCommercialTerms() previously allowed re-approval with DIFFERENT values indefinitely, even after a contract/invoice/subscription had already been created from a prior approval — an authoritative-state/ledger-state divergence with no record of which approval produced which artifact. Fixed: exported the existing pilotHasFinancialArtifacts() census (lib/pilot/pilot-ownership.ts, previously private) and made approveCommercialTerms() refuse ANY further approval (409, even with identical values) once a real financial artifact exists for the pilot, checked AFTER the SAME row lock used for the write (TOCTOU-safe against a concurrent commercial-transition). (4) TERMS SURVIVED ORGANIZATION REBIND — rebindPilotOrganization() changed verifiedOrganizationId/verifiedBy/verifiedAt but left a prior organization's approved commercial terms intact, so commercial-transition could create the NEW organization's financial artifacts from an approval made under the PREVIOUS organization's context. Fixed: rebind now unconditionally clears verifiedMemberCount/verifiedPilotAmount/verifiedSubscriptionPlanId/commercialTermsApprovedBy/commercialTermsApprovedAt whenever the verified organization actually changes (never for the idempotent same-org no-op path), forcing fresh approval under the new organization's context before any further financial-artifact-creating transition. Also closed two smaller financial-hardening gaps: pilotAmount is now validated on its NORMALIZED (toFixed(2)-rounded) value — at least $0.01 and within numeric(12,2) bounds — not the raw pre-rounding input (a raw value like 0.001 was previously positive but normalized to "0.00"); and commercial-transition's subscription_active branch now revalidates the approved plan's isActive status inside the SAME locked transaction at ACTIVATION time, not just at approval time, staging the activation only (never silently proceeding) if the plan has since been deactivated. Round 27 closed 3 further lifecycle gaps an independent review found in round 26's own delivery: (1) TERMS APPROVABLE BEFORE ORGANIZATION VERIFICATION — round 26 correctly cleared commercial terms on rebindPilotOrganization (an already-verified org changing to a different one), but approveCommercialTerms() never checked verifiedOrganizationId at all, so terms could be approved while the pilot's organization was still NULL (never yet verified), then bindPilotOrganization() (the first-time NULL -> org bind, a SEPARATE function from rebind) could bind it afterward with the pre-existing approval never evaluated in that organization's context. Fixed: approveCommercialTerms() now loads verifiedOrganizationId inside its own locked pilot read and returns 409 if absent, closing the gap for the FIRST bind the same way round 26 closed it for rebinds. (2) ACKNOWLEDGED POST-ARTIFACT REBIND CREATED A PERMANENT DEAD END — rebindPilotOrganization() still permitted an organization change after financial artifacts existed via an acknowledgeFinancialArtifacts=true escape hatch, which then unconditionally cleared the pilot's commercial terms (round 26) — but round 26 ALSO made approveCommercialTerms() refuse EVERY further approval once any financial artifact exists. Combined, an acknowledged rebind cleared the terms and then made re-approving them permanently impossible, since the pre-existing artifact is never deleted. Fixed: removed the acknowledgeFinancialArtifacts escape hatch entirely — rebindPilotOrganization() now unconditionally refuses (409, no override) once any real financial artifact exists; a post-artifact organization correction requires a dedicated financial-correction workflow that does not exist yet, not this function with an acknowledgement flag. (3) FINANCIAL ARTIFACTS DID NOT CARRY THE APPROVAL THAT PRODUCED THEM — commercialContracts/platformInvoices/orgSubscriptions metadata recorded only { source, pilotApplicationId }, so once an organization correction cleared the pilot row's own terms (round 26), a previously-created contract or invoice could no longer prove which approved commercial snapshot produced it. Fixed: new buildCommercialTermsSnapshot() (lib/pilot/commercialization-wave1.ts, reusing the SAME deterministic DJB2-style checksum already used for artifact/reference version records) builds an immutable { verifiedOrganizationId, verifiedMemberCount, verifiedPilotAmount, verifiedSubscriptionPlanId, commercialTermsApprovedBy, commercialTermsApprovedAt } snapshot plus a commercialTermsFingerprint hash, stamped into the metadata of every commercialContracts / platformInvoices / platformInvoiceLineItems / orgSubscriptions row CREATED (not merely updated) by commercial-transition — the pilot row's own terms remain the CURRENT authoritative snapshot; each artifact's stamped snapshot is the HISTORICAL one in effect at the moment that specific artifact was created, and the two are expected to diverge over time after any correction, which is exactly what this makes provable. Round 28 closed the one concrete provenance bypass an independent review found in round 27's own creation-side stamping: SUBSCRIPTION PROVENANCE WAS MUTABLE BY AN ORDINARY STEWARD — app/api/billing/subscriptions/[id]/route.ts's PATCH accepted `metadata: z.record(z.unknown()).optional()` at steward-level auth and wrote `.set({ ...body, updatedAt: new Date() })`, a full-column replace of orgSubscriptions.metadata — so a same-org steward could erase (`{"metadata":{}}`) or forge (fabricated snapshot + fingerprint) the commercialTermsSnapshot/commercialTermsFingerprint round 27 stamps at creation, defeating the provenance claim entirely (the fingerprint is deliberately non-cryptographic and lives in the SAME mutable JSON object it is meant to attest, so forging both together is trivial once the column itself is writable). Reviewed and confirmed contracts/invoices have no equivalent exposed arbitrary-metadata PATCH in this codebase — the defect was subscription-only. Fixed: the route now strips both server-owned keys from the client's metadata fragment (never trusting a client-supplied value for either, whether erased or forged) and restores each one from the row's CURRENT value (never an earlier read, never fabricated if the row never had it) — an ordinary steward may still freely edit any OTHER metadata key, but never these two. Also hardened the financial-transition gate itself: it previously verified verifiedMemberCount/verifiedPilotAmount/verifiedSubscriptionPlanId (round 25-27) but only TYPE-CAST commercialTermsApprovedBy/commercialTermsApprovedAt as non-null when building the provenance snapshot rather than actually checking them at runtime — since both DB columns are nullable, a partially populated or drifted row could in principle produce an artifact with incomplete provenance; the 409 gate now requires both fields non-null before any financial-artifact-creating transition, same as the other three fields.

canonicalAuthority.reason: Round 17 resolved this table; round 18 corrected dbExecutionPrincipal from TENANT_RUNTIME to MIXED (three authority modes: public unauthenticated INSERT, same-org steward SELECT/UPDATE/DELETE, platform system_admin+ cross-org SELECT/UPDATE) and moved platform-tier reads onto withSystemContext(). Round 19 closed three remaining trust-boundary gaps the round-18 review found: (1) AUTHORIZE-BEFORE-ELEVATE ORDERING — the round-18 collection GET called withSystemContext() first and relied on the generated crudRoutes handler's OWN internal auth check (buried inside withApi), so an unauthenticated/under-authorized request still opened a system-principal connection before being rejected; fixed by adding an explicit hasMinRole('system_admin') check in app/api/pilot/apply/route.ts BEFORE withSystemContext() is ever called. (2) RECORD-EXISTENCE ORACLE — lib/pilot/pilot-ownership.ts's withPilotOwnership() (wrapping app/api/pilot/apply/[id]/route.ts's GET/PATCH/DELETE) performed its system-scoped ownership-lookup BEFORE any auth check at all, so an unauthenticated caller's response differed (404 vs. an auth failure further downstream) depending on whether an arbitrary pilot id existed — a cross-tenant existence oracle, plus an unconditional system-principal SELECT triggered by requests that were never going to be allowed to proceed. Fixed: withPilotOwnership() now takes an explicit minRole option (default 'steward', matching [id]/route.ts's own crudRoutes config) and calls hasMinRole(minRole) FIRST, uniformly rejecting with 403 regardless of id existence, before touching the database at all. (3) CLAIMED VS. VERIFIED OWNERSHIP — responses.organizationId (the JSONB field this table's ownership model reads) is an unauthenticated client assertion from the public POST body, never server-attested identity; renamed the accessor from getPilotOwnerOrganizationId to getPilotClaimedOrganizationId with an explicit doc comment establishing that provenance. It remains acceptable to use for the LOW-STAKES same-org self-service access-control gate (a submitter can only ever act on the exact org they themselves claimed — no cross-tenant read is possible since a real member of that org must independently match the same claim), but app/api/pilot/apply/[id]/commercial-transition/route.ts — which creates REAL commercialContracts/billingAccounts/orgSubscriptions/platformInvoices keyed by that claim — now REQUIRES an independent platform-tier decision (authorizePilotAccess(...).reason === 'platform', i.e. system_admin+), not same-org self-service, before executing; same-org actors are correctly authorized elsewhere (viewing/editing their own submitted application) but can no longer self-provision billing records off their own unverified claim. Also made the public POST explicitly governed rather than public-by-omission: added to config/public-api-routes.ts + lib/public-routes.ts + zod schema validation + IP rate-limiting (5/hr), and added scripts/lib/api-route-governance-scanner.ts (a per-EXPORT, not per-file, static governance checker) plus scripts/__tests__/pilot-apply-per-export-governance.test.ts, which contains a hardcoded regression fixture proving the checker catches the EXACT original bug class (a crudRoutes-wrapped GET hiding a bare, wrapper-less POST in the same file) and asserts the whole app/api/pilot/** tree is now fully per-export governed. Round 20 closed the remaining trust-boundary gap the round-19 review found: 'platform review' proved WHO could approve a commercial transition, never that the CLAIMED organization was actually the real organization behind the application — commercial-transition still resolved billing off responses.organizationId (the unauthenticated claim), so a malicious public submitter could set responses.organizationId to a victim org's real id, and a legitimate platform reviewer approving the transition would still misattribute real billing/contract records to that victim. FIX: added a server-controlled `verified_organization_id`/`verified_by`/`verified_at` column set (Django migration backend/content/migrations/0002_pilotapplications_verified_organization.py — pilot_applications is a Django-canonical business entity per docs/categories/platform-and-operations/architecture/orm-governance/master-orm-governance-index.md, so the Drizzle schema addition in db/schema/domains/marketing.ts is a TYPE MIRROR only, not the migration source; validated via `manage.py makemigrations --check --dry-run` + `manage.py check`, both clean, no live DB available in this environment to actually apply it). New `getPilotVerifiedOrganizationId()` accessor (lib/pilot/pilot-ownership.ts) reads ONLY this column; new `bindPilotOrganization()` is the ONLY function permitted to write it, fails closed (404) if the target organization does not exist, runs under withSystemContext(). New platform-only endpoint POST /api/pilot/apply/[id]/verify-organization (system_admin+ before any DB access, matching the round-19 auth-ordering pattern) is the ONLY way to bind a pilot to a verified org — the public intake POST cannot set these fields (not in its zod schema, not in its insert values). commercial-transition/route.ts now reads ONLY getPilotVerifiedOrganizationId(application), never responses.organizationId, and returns 409 if the organization has not yet been verified — a platform reviewer's authorization decision no longer implicitly re-uses the submitter's own unverified claim as billing identity. Also replaced the round-19 in-memory (lib/rate-limit.ts, per-process Map, IP+User-Agent keyed) rate limiter on the public POST with the Redis/Upstash-backed, fail-closed lib/rate-limiter.ts's checkRateLimit() (new RATE_LIMITS_PER_IP.PILOT_APPLY preset, 5/hr) — the same distributed primitive already used for other public/abuse-prone endpoints, correctly shared across instances/restarts. Corrected scripts/lib/api-route-governance-scanner.ts: `rateLimit(`/`verifyTurnstileToken(` were REMOVED from AUTH_ESTABLISHING_IDENTIFIERS (rate limiting and anti-bot challenges are abuse controls, not authentication — a route calling ONLY rateLimit() before an unguarded sensitive operation must still be classified UNGOVERNED) and moved to a new, separate ABUSE_CONTROL_IDENTIFIERS list checked via `hasAbuseControl()`, used ONLY for an additive assertion on already-allowlisted public exports ("this public route also has a rate-limit/anti-bot control"), never as an alternate path to "governed". Two new regression fixtures in scripts/__tests__/pilot-apply-per-export-governance.test.ts prove a rate-limit-only (or checkRateLimit/Turnstile-only) handler is still flagged ungoverned. Eventual RLS design (not built this round — the 87-table policy-expansion migration remains blocked pending NEEDS_REVIEW=0): once verified_organization_id exists as a real column (not JSONB), the eventual tenant RLS policy can reference it directly (`verified_organization_id = current_setting('app.current_org_id')::uuid`) rather than the fragile JSONB-path expression originally sketched in round 18/19, plus an explicit system-role policy (`TO union_eyes_system`, unconditional) for platform operations — this classification's MIXED dbExecutionPrincipal already reflects that eventual split. A live-DB proof that withSystemContext actually reaches the system connection, and that the Django migration applies cleanly, requires a real Postgres instance (rls:verify --mode=full / manage.py migrate), not available in this environment; the source-level correctness (correct auth ordering, correct wrapper on the correct decision branch, migration matches model per makemigrations --check) is the property asserted by this round's regression tests. Round 21 closed two further gaps an independent live-repo review found: (1) SERVER-CONTROLLED FIELDS WERE NOT SERVER-WRITE-ONLY — the generic PATCH on app/api/pilot/apply/[id]/route.ts (crudRoutes with no blockedPatchFields) let a same-org steward set verifiedOrganizationId/verifiedBy/verifiedAt directly, bypassing both the platform-only verify-organization endpoint and bindPilotOrganization() entirely; fixed by adding blockedPatchFields: ['verifiedOrganizationId','verifiedBy','verifiedAt','status','reviewedAt','approvedAt'] (status/reviewedAt/approvedAt are also exclusively FSM-governed by commercial-transition, not arbitrary steward-editable fields), backed by a new exported, directly-unit-tested stripBlockedPatchFields() helper in lib/api/crud-factory.ts. (2) UNBOUNDED REBIND LIFECYCLE — bindPilotOrganization() previously overwrote an existing binding unconditionally, permitting Org A verified -> financial activity begins -> silently rebound to Org B -> subsequent commercial transitions misattributed to Org B; fixed by making the bind immutable (idempotent no-op for the SAME org, 409 for a DIFFERENT org) and adding a separate, deliberately-friction-ful rebindPilotOrganization() correction primitive (app/api/pilot/apply/[id]/rebind-organization/route.ts, system_admin+ only) that requires a non-empty audit reason and refuses to proceed when a commercialContracts row already exists for the pilot unless the caller explicitly passes acknowledgeFinancialArtifacts=true (which does NOT itself migrate those rows — a deliberate, logged, audited correction, not silent reattribution). Also corrected the RED-TEAM-ORG-011 static ratchet in security/redteam/ue-org-scope-fuzz.test.ts: its stale getPilotOwnerOrganizationId marker (renamed in round 19) is fixed, and it now recognizes platform CONTROL-PLANE pilot routes (verify-organization, rebind-organization) as requiring a canonical platform-admin guard (hasMinRole('system_admin') / PILOT_PLATFORM_ACCESS_MIN_LEVEL) instead of a same-org OWNERSHIP marker, since same-org self-service was never the correct model for those two routes. Separately, confirmed the demo deployment profile (DJANGO_SKIP_MIGRATIONS=true per .github/workflows/deploy-union-eyes.yml) does not automatically apply this table's migrations; added backend/content/management/commands/check_pilot_schema.py as an explicit, narrowly-scoped preflight ops can run against any environment before serving pilot traffic there. Round 22 closed four further bounded gaps an independent review found directly inside this trust boundary: (1) MUTABLE CLAIMED-ORG FIELD — responses.organizationId (the JSONB claim getPilotClaimedOrganizationId reads for ordinary same-org access) was not protected by round 21's blockedPatchFields (a flat top-level-key list can't reach a nested JSONB subfield) — a same-org steward could pass the ownership pre-check on Org A's row, then PATCH responses.organizationId to Org B, transferring subsequent same-org access with no platform involvement at all. Fixed via a new crud-factory beforeUpdate hook (mirrors the existing beforeCreate pattern) wired to a new exported, directly-unit-tested preserveClaimedOrganizationOnPatch(), which forces the claimed organizationId back to the row's existing value on every PATCH regardless of what the client sends, while leaving every other responses subfield ordinarily editable. (2) INCOMPLETE FINANCIAL-ARTIFACT CENSUS — rebindPilotOrganization() only checked commercialContracts, but commercial-transition's invoice_issued/subscription_active branches (reachable via allowSkip) can each create a real platformInvoices/orgSubscriptions row independently of contract_sent, so a pilot could carry a real invoice or subscription with no contract and rebind would proceed without acknowledgeFinancialArtifacts. Fixed via a new pilotHasFinancialArtifacts() helper checking all three tables by their shared metadata->>pilotApplicationId marker. (3) NO CONCURRENCY GUARD — bindPilotOrganization/rebindPilotOrganization performed read-then-update with no row lock, so two concurrent verifications for different orgs (or a rebind racing a concurrent commercial-transition creating a financial artifact) could both observe stale state; last writer wins. Fixed: both functions now take SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on the pilot row inside withSystemContext's real transaction, and commercial-transition's monetization transaction takes the same lock before creating any artifact, so all three now serialize against each other. (4) BROKEN GENERIC DELETE — the shared factory's DELETE soft-deletes by writing status='archived' whenever a status column exists, but round 21 made pilot status exclusively FSM-governed by commercial-transition, and pilot_status has no 'archived' value at all — the exported DELETE handler both violated the new FSM rule and would fail against the enum if ever invoked. Fixed by removing the DELETE export entirely (405 by default); a real archive/close action belongs in the commercial-transition FSM, not a generic soft-delete. Also corrected overstated language from round 21: rebindPilotOrganization's logging is a structured logger.warn call, not yet a durable audit_logs row — doc comments now say "logged for traceability," not "audited." Round 23 closed three further gaps a deeper live-source review found directly inside this trust boundary: (1) LOCKED TOO LATE — commercial-transition previously loaded the application, derived verifiedOrganizationId/responses/fromState, and validated the FSM transition BEFORE entering the transaction that locks the row, then used those pre-lock values inside the lock — so a rebind that committed between the initial read and the lock being acquired left the transition using a stale verified-org/commercial-state snapshot. Fixed: the row is now re-SELECTed with FOR UPDATE as the FIRST statement inside the transaction, and verifiedOrganizationId, responses, fromState, and the proposal are ALL derived from that locked read; a new CommercialTransitionRejected error class lets expected rejections (404/409/400) discovered after locking roll back the transaction and still return the exact intended HTTP response. The earlier pre-lock read is now only a cheap existence + role-tier check, never a source of financial or FSM decisions. (2) RESPONSES REMAINED A MIXED-TRUST STORE — round 22 protected only responses.organizationId from steward PATCH, leaving responses.commercialState (drives FSM validation), responses.subscriptionPlanId (selects the billing plan on activation), commercialTransitionHistory, pilotIntelligence, qualification/opportunity scores, artifact-version metadata, and commercialMonetization all editable — contradicting round 21's claim that commercial state is FSM-controlled. Fixed: preserveClaimedOrganizationOnPatch was generalized into preserveServerOwnedResponsesFields, which restores ALL server-owned responses keys (organizationId plus the full commercial/scoring/artifact list above) to their existing values on every PATCH, while leaving every other responses key ordinarily editable. (3) TENANT AUTHORIZATION STILL FOLLOWED THE CLAIM AFTER VERIFICATION/REBIND — the ownership pre-check loaded only responses and authorized via getPilotClaimedOrganizationId, never verifiedOrganizationId, so after a platform rebind moved the authoritative owner from Org A to Org B, Org A stewards still passed the tenant ownership check and Org B stewards did not — the rebind changed financial identity but not tenant authorization. Fixed: a new getPilotEffectiveOrganizationId () (verifiedOrganizationId ?? claimedOrganizationId) is now the ONLY value application-layer ownership checks use (enforcePilotOwnership/withPilotOwnership, and loadPilotApplicationForOwnershipCheck now also selects verifiedOrganizationId to make this possible); once a verified owner exists it is authoritative everywhere, including after a rebind. The eventual tenant RLS policy for this table must encode the SAME effective-owner rule (COALESCE(verified_organization_id, (responses->>'organizationId')::uuid) = current_setting(...)), not the claim-only JSONB expression sketched in earlier rounds. Round 24 was structural rather than another field-by-field patch: (1) PUBLIC-CREATE PROVENANCE BYPASS — the public intake POST's responses: z.record(z.unknown()) schema let an unauthenticated applicant seed a brand-new row with the SAME reserved keys rounds 22-23 protected on UPDATE (commercialState, subscriptionPlanId, qualification scores, artifact metadata, ...), and the PATCH-time protection then faithfully preserved that attacker-seeded value forever — protecting an update is meaningless if creation was never sanitized. Fixed by extracting a SINGLE canonical registry (lib/pilot/responses-authority.ts's RESERVED_RESPONSES_KEYS) used by BOTH the public POST (sanitizeResponsesForPublicCreate strips every reserved key except organizationId, the intentionally untrusted claim) and the PATCH path, so there is exactly one place to update when a new governed route starts writing a new responses key. (2) INCOMPLETE REGISTRY — round 23's list missed reference-profile/route.ts's 4 reference-version keys (pilotReferenceVersions, latestPilotReferenceVersionId, latestPilotReferenceChecksum, latestPilotReferenceUpdatedAt) entirely — verified via a full-repo inventory of every '.update(pilotApplications)' call site this round; all 4 now reserved. championScore/activityScore deliberately remain unreserved — verified no route ever WRITES them (only reads, as optional bounded-impact scoring inputs with a computed fallback when absent), so reserving them would remove the only way they can ever be set; documented as a deliberate decision, not an oversight. (3) PATCH COULD STILL REVERT FRESHLY COMMITTED SERVER STATE — the round 22/23 beforeUpdate hook read the current row, copied reserved values into the merged object, then replaced the WHOLE responses column — a lost-update race if commercial-transition committed a reserved-key change between that read and this PATCH's write (the PATCH would silently revert it). Fixed by replacing the read-copy-write model with an atomic JSONB MERGE: crudRoutes() gained a mergeJsonColumns option (lib/api/crud-factory.ts) that locks the row FOR UPDATE, strips reserved keys from the client's responses fragment (never reading or reproducing their current values), and issues 'responses || fragment' rather than a full-column replace — a concurrent write to any key absent from the fragment can never be reverted, because the PATCH's SQL never mentions that key at all. Round 25 closed 4 structural gaps the reviewer found in this model: (1) the merge helper silently fell back to a full-column REPLACE for a non-object responses value (e.g. an array or null) — buildMergeSetValues() now throws via validateMergeJsonColumnValues() for any mergeJsonColumns value that is not a plain object, closing a direct reserved-state destruction primitive; (2) intelligence/artifacts/reference-profile's POST handlers ran an UNLOCKED read-modify-write on the whole responses column — a server-writer-vs-server-writer race against commercial-transition's own locked write — now rewritten onto a new withLockedPilotMutation() primitive (lib/pilot/pilot-mutation.ts) that locks the row FOR UPDATE, re-authorizes the effective owner under that SAME lock, and merges only the specific keys each route owns (pilotIntelligence; the 4 artifact-version fields; the 4 reference-version fields), never the whole column; (3) the generic CRUD PATCH's ownership pre-check ran on an unlocked read BEFORE crud-factory's own row lock — a concurrent platform rebind could move ownership in that gap — closed via a new lockedAuthCheck CrudOptions hook that re-evaluates authorizePilotAccess against the row the SAME transaction just locked; (4) commercial-transition derived real contract/invoice amounts from applicant-supplied member_count (steward-PATCH-editable) and selected a subscription plan via an ambiguous "any active plan" fallback since responses.subscriptionPlanId had no governed writer — both replaced by a platform-approved commercial-terms snapshot (verified_member_count, verified_pilot_amount, verified_subscription_plan_id, commercial_terms_approved_by/at columns; lib/pilot/commercial-terms-authority.ts's approveCommercialTerms, the ONLY writer, gated behind system_admin+ like verify-organization/rebind-organization) that every financial-artifact-creating transition (contract_sent, invoice_issued, subscription_active) now requires before proceeding. Round 26 closed lifecycle/governance defects an independent review found in round 25's own delivery: (1) ORM AUTHORITY DOCTRINE VIOLATION — round 25 added the 5 commercial-terms columns via a standalone raw SQL file in apps/union-eyes/db/migrations/, which is BOTH a frozen, read-only historical Drizzle lineage (db/migrations/.lineage-frozen — new files there are explicitly prohibited per db/migrations/LINEAGE-FROZEN.md) AND a violation of this table's own Django-canonical authority (this table is a Django-canonical business entity per docs/categories/platform-and-operations/architecture/orm-governance/master-orm-governance-index.md; Drizzle's marketing.ts is a TYPE MIRROR only). Fixed: deleted the standalone SQL file; added the 5 fields to Django's PilotApplications model (backend/content/models.py) and a real Django migration (backend/content/migrations/0003_pilotapplications_commercial_terms.py), validated via `manage.py makemigrations --check --dry-run` + `manage.py check` (both clean for this table; a small set of PRE-EXISTING, unrelated drift in other Django apps — auth_core, content/documents-rename, core, services, unions — remains exactly as it was before this round, confirmed unchanged, not silently fixed as part of this round). (2) STALE DEMO SCHEMA PREFLIGHT — backend/content/management/commands/check_pilot_schema.py still only checked the 3 round-21 verified-organization columns, so it could report success on a database where every round-25 commercial-transition call to a financial-artifact-creating state would 500 on "column does not exist"; expanded to check all 8 columns across both migrations, with a column-to-migration map so a failure names the exact migration(s) still needed. (3) COMMERCIAL TERMS APPROVED BUT NOT LIFECYCLE-BOUND — approveCommercialTerms() previously allowed re-approval with DIFFERENT values indefinitely, even after a contract/invoice/subscription had already been created from a prior approval — an authoritative-state/ledger-state divergence with no record of which approval produced which artifact. Fixed: exported the existing pilotHasFinancialArtifacts() census (lib/pilot/pilot-ownership.ts, previously private) and made approveCommercialTerms() refuse ANY further approval (409, even with identical values) once a real financial artifact exists for the pilot, checked AFTER the SAME row lock used for the write (TOCTOU-safe against a concurrent commercial-transition). (4) TERMS SURVIVED ORGANIZATION REBIND — rebindPilotOrganization() changed verifiedOrganizationId/verifiedBy/verifiedAt but left a prior organization's approved commercial terms intact, so commercial-transition could create the NEW organization's financial artifacts from an approval made under the PREVIOUS organization's context. Fixed: rebind now unconditionally clears verifiedMemberCount/verifiedPilotAmount/verifiedSubscriptionPlanId/commercialTermsApprovedBy/commercialTermsApprovedAt whenever the verified organization actually changes (never for the idempotent same-org no-op path), forcing fresh approval under the new organization's context before any further financial-artifact-creating transition. Also closed two smaller financial-hardening gaps: pilotAmount is now validated on its NORMALIZED (toFixed(2)-rounded) value — at least $0.01 and within numeric(12,2) bounds — not the raw pre-rounding input (a raw value like 0.001 was previously positive but normalized to "0.00"); and commercial-transition's subscription_active branch now revalidates the approved plan's isActive status inside the SAME locked transaction at ACTIVATION time, not just at approval time, staging the activation only (never silently proceeding) if the plan has since been deactivated. Round 27 closed 3 further lifecycle gaps an independent review found in round 26's own delivery: (1) TERMS APPROVABLE BEFORE ORGANIZATION VERIFICATION — round 26 correctly cleared commercial terms on rebindPilotOrganization (an already-verified org changing to a different one), but approveCommercialTerms() never checked verifiedOrganizationId at all, so terms could be approved while the pilot's organization was still NULL (never yet verified), then bindPilotOrganization() (the first-time NULL -> org bind, a SEPARATE function from rebind) could bind it afterward with the pre-existing approval never evaluated in that organization's context. Fixed: approveCommercialTerms() now loads verifiedOrganizationId inside its own locked pilot read and returns 409 if absent, closing the gap for the FIRST bind the same way round 26 closed it for rebinds. (2) ACKNOWLEDGED POST-ARTIFACT REBIND CREATED A PERMANENT DEAD END — rebindPilotOrganization() still permitted an organization change after financial artifacts existed via an acknowledgeFinancialArtifacts=true escape hatch, which then unconditionally cleared the pilot's commercial terms (round 26) — but round 26 ALSO made approveCommercialTerms() refuse EVERY further approval once any financial artifact exists. Combined, an acknowledged rebind cleared the terms and then made re-approving them permanently impossible, since the pre-existing artifact is never deleted. Fixed: removed the acknowledgeFinancialArtifacts escape hatch entirely — rebindPilotOrganization() now unconditionally refuses (409, no override) once any real financial artifact exists; a post-artifact organization correction requires a dedicated financial-correction workflow that does not exist yet, not this function with an acknowledgement flag. (3) FINANCIAL ARTIFACTS DID NOT CARRY THE APPROVAL THAT PRODUCED THEM — commercialContracts/platformInvoices/orgSubscriptions metadata recorded only { source, pilotApplicationId }, so once an organization correction cleared the pilot row's own terms (round 26), a previously-created contract or invoice could no longer prove which approved commercial snapshot produced it. Fixed: new buildCommercialTermsSnapshot() (lib/pilot/commercialization-wave1.ts, reusing the SAME deterministic DJB2-style checksum already used for artifact/reference version records) builds an immutable { verifiedOrganizationId, verifiedMemberCount, verifiedPilotAmount, verifiedSubscriptionPlanId, commercialTermsApprovedBy, commercialTermsApprovedAt } snapshot plus a commercialTermsFingerprint hash, stamped into the metadata of every commercialContracts / platformInvoices / platformInvoiceLineItems / orgSubscriptions row CREATED (not merely updated) by commercial-transition — the pilot row's own terms remain the CURRENT authoritative snapshot; each artifact's stamped snapshot is the HISTORICAL one in effect at the moment that specific artifact was created, and the two are expected to diverge over time after any correction, which is exactly what this makes provable. Round 28 closed the one concrete provenance bypass an independent review found in round 27's own creation-side stamping: SUBSCRIPTION PROVENANCE WAS MUTABLE BY AN ORDINARY STEWARD — app/api/billing/subscriptions/[id]/route.ts's PATCH accepted `metadata: z.record(z.unknown()).optional()` at steward-level auth and wrote `.set({ ...body, updatedAt: new Date() })`, a full-column replace of orgSubscriptions.metadata — so a same-org steward could erase (`{"metadata":{}}`) or forge (fabricated snapshot + fingerprint) the commercialTermsSnapshot/commercialTermsFingerprint round 27 stamps at creation, defeating the provenance claim entirely (the fingerprint is deliberately non-cryptographic and lives in the SAME mutable JSON object it is meant to attest, so forging both together is trivial once the column itself is writable). Reviewed and confirmed contracts/invoices have no equivalent exposed arbitrary-metadata PATCH in this codebase — the defect was subscription-only. Fixed: the route now strips both server-owned keys from the client's metadata fragment (never trusting a client-supplied value for either, whether erased or forged) and restores each one from the row's CURRENT value (never an earlier read, never fabricated if the row never had it) — an ordinary steward may still freely edit any OTHER metadata key, but never these two. Also hardened the financial-transition gate itself: it previously verified verifiedMemberCount/verifiedPilotAmount/verifiedSubscriptionPlanId (round 25-27) but only TYPE-CAST commercialTermsApprovedBy/commercialTermsApprovedAt as non-null when building the provenance snapshot rather than actually checking them at runtime — since both DB columns are nullable, a partially populated or drifted row could in principle produce an artifact with incomplete provenance; the 409 gate now requires both fields non-null before any financial-artifact-creating transition, same as the other three fields.
